entries.64c53e19ebf60b7a1a68dcb5fcc1373bd7f79312: <div sID="gen19755" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Hos.5" sID="Hos.5"/> <div eID="gen19755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19756" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19757" type="x-p"/> The scope of this chapter is the same with that of the foregoing chapter, to discover the sin both of Israel and Judah, and to denounce the judgments of God against them. I. They are called to hearken to the charge, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.8">8</reference>. II. They are accused of many sins, which are here aggravated. 1. Persecution, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.7">ver. 7</reference>. 5. The tyranny of the princes, and the tameness of the people in submitting to it, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.10-Hos.5.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>. III. They are threatened with God's displeasure for their sins; he knows all their wickedness (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.3">ver. 3</reference>) and makes known his wrath against them for it, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.9">ver. 9</reference>. 1. They shall fall in their iniquity, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.5">ver. 5</reference>. 2. God will forsake them, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.6">ver. 6</reference>. 3. Their portions shall be devoured, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.7">ver. 7</reference>. 4. God will rebuke them, and pour out his wrath upon them, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.9-Hos.5.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>. 5. They shall be oppressed, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.11">ver. 11</reference>. 6. God will be as a moth to them in secret judgments (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.12">ver. 12</reference>) and as a lion in public judgments, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.14">ver. 14</reference>. IV. They are blamed for the wrong course they took under their afflictions, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.13">ver. 13</reference>. V. It is intimated that they shall at length take a right course, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.15">ver. 15</reference>. The more generally these things are expressed of so much the more general use they are for our learning, and particularly for our admonition.
entries.ba9228071bef3dfb37f1da800e87cc3b97f5ec4e: <div eID="gen19757" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19756" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Charge against Israel and Judah; Judgments Threatened. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 758.)</title> <div sID="gen19758" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Hear ye this, O priests; and hearken, ye house of Israel; and give ye ear, O house of the king; for judgment <hi type="italic">is</hi> toward you, because ye have been a snare on Mizpah, and a net spread upon Tabor. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the revolters are profound to make slaughter, though I <hi type="italic">have been</hi> a rebuker of them all. <hi type="super">3</hi> I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hid from me: for now, O Ephraim, thou committest whoredom, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Israel is defiled. <hi type="super">4</hi> They will not frame their doings to turn unto their God: for the spirit of whoredoms <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the midst of them, and they have not known the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">5</hi> And the pride of Israel doth testify to his face: therefore shall Israel and Ephraim fall in their iniquity; Judah also shall fall with them. <hi type="super">6</hi> They shall go with their flocks and with their herds to seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; but they shall not find <hi type="italic">him;</hi> he hath withdrawn himself from them. <hi type="super">7</hi> They have dealt treacherously against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : for they have begotten strange children: now shall a month devour them with their portions. <div eID="gen19758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19759" type="x-p"/> Here, I. All orders and degrees of men are cited to appear and answer to such things as shall be laid to their charge (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Hear you this, O priests!</hi> whether <hi type="italic">in holy orders</hi> (as those in Judah, and perhaps many in Israel too, for in the ten tribes there were divers cities of priests and Levites, who, it is probable, staid in their own lot after the revolt of the ten tribes and did so much of their office as might be done at a distance from the temple) or <hi type="italic">pretending holy orders,</hi> as the priests of the calves, who, some think, are included here. "Hearken, <hi type="italic">you house of Israel,</hi> the common people, and <hi type="italic">give ear, O house of the king!</hi>" let them all take notice, for they have all contributed to the national guilt, and they shall all share in the national judgments. Note, If neither the sanctity of the priesthood nor the dignity of the royal family will prevail to keep out sin, it cannot be expected that they should avail to keep out wrath. If the priests, and the house of the king, though they bear such noble characters, sin like others, their noble characters will not excuse them, but they must smart like others. Nor shall it be any plea for <hi type="italic">the house of Israel</hi> that they were misled by their priests and princes, but they shall receive their doom with them, and neither their meanness nor their multitude shall be their exemption. <div eID="gen19759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19760" type="x-p"/> II. Witness is produced against them, one instead of a thousand; it is God's omniscience (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me.</hi> They have <hi type="italic">not known the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.4">v. 4</reference>), but the Lord has known them, knows their true character however disguised, knows their secret wickedness however concealed. Note, Men's rejecting the knowledge of God will not secure them from his knowledge of them; and when he contends with them he will prove their sins upon them by his own knowledge, so that is will be in vain to plead <hi type="italic">Not guilty.</hi> <div eID="gen19760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19761" type="x-p"/> III. Very bad things are laid to their charge. 1. They had been very ingenious and very industrious to draw people either into sin or into trouble: You have been <hi type="italic">a snare on Mizpah, and a net spread upon Tabor</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.1">v. 1</reference>), that is, such snares and nets as the huntsmen used to lay upon those mountains in pursuit of their game. When the worship of the calves was set up in Israel the patrons of that idolatry, and sticklers for it, contrived by all possible arts and wiles to draw men into it and reconcile those to it that at first had a dread of it. Note, Those that allure and entice men to sin, however they may pretend friendship and good-will, are to be looked upon as <hi type="italic">snares and nets</hi> to them, and <hi type="italic">their hands as bands,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.26">Eccl. vii. 26</reference>. But to those whom they could not seduce into sin they were as a net and a snare to bring them into trouble. Some think it was their practice to set spies in the road, and particularly upon the mountains of Mizpah and Tabor, at the times of the solemn feasts at Jerusalem, to watch if any of their people who were piously affected went thither, and to inform against them, that they might be prosecuted for it, thus doing the devil's work, who disquiets those whom he cannot debauch. 2. They had been both very crafty and very cruel in carrying on their designs (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">The revolters are profound to make slaughter.</hi> Note, Those who have themselves apostatized from the truths of God are often the most subtle and barbarous persecutors of those who still adhere to them. Nothing will serve them but to <hi type="italic">make slaughter</hi> (it is the blood of the saints that they thirst after): and with the serpent's sting they have his head; they are <hi type="italic">profound</hi> to do it. O the depth of <hi type="italic">the depths of Satan,</hi> of the wickedness of his agents, of those that have <hi type="italic">deeply revolted!</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.31.6">Isa. xxxi. 6</reference>. Now that which aggravated this was the many reproofs and warnings that had been given them: <hi type="italic">Though I have been a rebuker of them all.</hi> The prophet had been so, a reprover by office. He had many a time told them of the evil of their ways and doings, had dealt plainly <hi type="italic">with them all,</hi> and had not spared either the priests or the house of the king. God himself had been <hi type="italic">a rebuker of them all</hi> by their own consciences and by his providences. Note, Sins against reproof are doubly sinful, <reference osisRef="Prov.29.1">Prov. xxix. 1</reference>. 3. They had <hi type="italic">committed whoredom,</hi> had defiled their own bodies with fleshly lusts, had defiled their own souls with the worship of idols, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.3">v. 3</reference>. This God was a witness to, though secretly committed and artfully palliated. Nay, the piercing eye of God saw <hi type="italic">the spirit of whoredom</hi> that was <hi type="italic">in the midst of them,</hi> their secret inclination and disposition to those sins, the love they had to their sins, and the dominion their sins had over them, how much they were under the power of a <hi type="italic">spirit of whoredom,</hi> that <hi type="italic">root of bitterness</hi> which bore all this gall and wormwood, that corrupt and poisoned fountain. 4. They had no disposition at all to come into acquaintance and communion with God. The <hi type="italic">spirit of whoredoms,</hi> having <hi type="italic">caused them to err</hi> from him, keeps them wandering endlessly, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.4">v. 4</reference>. (1.) They <hi type="italic">have not known the Lord,</hi> nor desire to know him, but have rather declined, nay dreaded, the knowledge of him, for that would disturb them in their sinful ways. (2.) Therefore <hi type="italic">they will not frame their doings to turn to their God,</hi> by which it appeared that they did not know him aright. This intimates their obstinate persistence in their apostasy from God; they would not <hi type="italic">turn to God,</hi> though he was <hi type="italic">their God,</hi> theirs in covenant, by whose name they had been called, and whom they were bound to <hi type="italic">serve.</hi> They would not return to the worship of him, from which they had turned aside. Nay, <hi type="italic">they would not frame their doings to turn to God.</hi> They would not <hi type="italic">consider their ways,</hi> nor dispose themselves into a serious temper, nor apply their minds to think of those things that would bring them to God. It is true we cannot by our own power, without the special grace of God, turn to him; but we may by the due improvement of our faculties, and the common aids of his Spirit, <hi type="italic">frame our doings</hi> to turn to him. Those that will not do this, that <hi type="italic">prepare not their hearts to seek the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.12.14">2 Chron. xii. 14</reference>), owe it to themselves that they are not turned; they die because they will die; and to those that will do this further grace shall not be wanting. (5.) They were guilty of notorious arrogancy, and insolence in sin (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">The pride of Israel doth testify to his face,</hi> doth witness against him that he is a rebel to God and his government. The <hi type="italic">spirit of whoredoms</hi> which was <hi type="italic">in the midst of them</hi> showed itself in the gaiety and gaudiness of their worship, as a harlot is known by her attire, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.10">Prov. vii. 10</reference>. The wantonness of her dress testifies to her face that she is not a modest woman. Or their pride in confronting the prophets God sent them and the message they brought (<reference osisRef="Jer.43.2">Jer. xliii. 2</reference>), or a haughty scornful conduct towards their brethren and those that were under them, <hi type="italic">witnessed against</hi> them that they were not God's people and justified God in all the humbling judgments he brought upon them. His pride testifies <hi type="italic">in his face;</hi> so some read it, agreeing with <reference osisRef="Isa.3.9">Isa. iii. 9</reference>, <hi type="italic">The show of their countenance doth witness against them.</hi> They have that <hi type="italic">proud look</hi> which <hi type="italic">the Lord hates.</hi> (6.) They departed from God to idols, and bred up their children in idolatry (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">They have dealt treacherously against the Lord,</hi> as a wife, who, in contempt of the marriage covenant, forsakes her husband, and lives in adultery with another. Thus those who are guilty of spiritual idolatry, whose god is their money, whose god is their belly, <hi type="italic">deal treacherously against the Lord;</hi> they violate their engagements to him and frustrate his expectations from them. Note, Wilful sinners are treacherous dealers. <hi type="italic">They have begotten strange children,</hi> that is, their children which they have begotten are estranged from God, and trained up in a false way of worship; they are a spurious brood, as <hi type="italic">children of fornication</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.8.41">John viii. 41</reference>), whom God will disown. Note, Those deal treacherously with God indeed who not only turn from following him themselves but train up their children in wicked ways. <div eID="gen19761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19762" type="x-p"/> IV. Very sad things are made to be their doom. In general (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.1">v. 1</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Judgment is towards you.</hi> God is coming forth to contend with you, and to testify his displeasure against you for your sins." It is time to hearken when judgment is towards us. In particular, <div eID="gen19762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19763" type="x-p"/> 1. They shall <hi type="italic">fall in their iniquity.</hi> This follows upon their <hi type="italic">pride testifying to their face</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.5">v. 5</reference>) <hi type="italic">Therefore shall Israel and Ephraim fall in their iniquity.</hi> Note, Pride will have a fall; it is the certain presage and forerunner of it. Those that exalt themselves shall be abased. The face in which pride testifies shall be filled with confusion. They shall not only fall, but fall in their iniquity, the saddest fall of any. Their pride kept them from repenting of their iniquity, and therefore they shall fall in it. Note, Those that are not humbled for their sins are likely to perish for ever in their sins. It is added, <hi type="italic">Judah also shall fall with them</hi> in her iniquity. As the ten tribes were carried captive into Assyria, for their idolatry, so the two tribes, in process of time, were carried into Babylon for following their bad example; but the former fell and were utterly cast down, the latter fell and were raised up again. Judah had the temple and priesthood, and yet these shall not secure them, but, if they sin with Israel and Ephraim, with them they shall fall. <div eID="gen19763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19764" type="x-p"/> 2. They shall fall short of God's favour when they profess to seek it (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall go with their flocks and with their herds to seek the Lord,</hi> but in vain; <hi type="italic">they shall not find him.</hi> This seems to be spoken principally of Judah, when they fell into their iniquity, and when they fell in their iniquity. (1.) When they fell into their iniquity they <hi type="italic">sought the Lord;</hi> but they did not <hi type="italic">seek him only,</hi> and therefore he was not <hi type="italic">found of them.</hi> When they worshipped strange gods, yet they kept up the show and shadow of the worship of the true God; they went as usual, at the solemn feasts, <hi type="italic">with their flocks and herds to seek the Lord;</hi> but their hearts were not <hi type="italic">upright with him,</hi> because they were not <hi type="italic">entire for him,</hi> and therefore he would not accept them; for <hi type="italic">then</hi> only shall we find him when we <hi type="italic">seek him with our whole heart,</hi> not divided between God and Baal, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.3">Ezek. xiv. 3</reference>. (2.) When they fell in their iniquity, or found themselves falling by it, they <hi type="italic">sought the Lord;</hi> but they did not seek him <hi type="italic">early,</hi> and therefore he will not be found of them. They shall see ruin coming upon them, and shall then, in their distress, flee to God, and think to make him their friend with burnt-offerings and sacrifices; but it will be too late then to turn away his wrath when <hi type="italic">the decree has gone forth.</hi> Even Josiah's reformation did not prevail to <hi type="italic">turn away the wrath of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.25-2Kgs.23.26">2 Kings xxiii. 25, 26</reference>. Those that go <hi type="italic">with their flocks and their herds</hi> only to seek the Lord, and not with their hearts and souls, cannot expect to find him, for his favour is not to be purchased with <hi type="italic">thousands of rams.</hi> Nor shall those speed who do not seek the Lord <hi type="italic">while he may be found,</hi> for there is a time when he will not be found. They shall not find him, for he has withdrawn himself; he will not be enquired of by them, but will turn a deaf ear to their sacrifices. See how much it is our concern to seek God early, now while the accepted time is, and the day of salvation. <div eID="gen19764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19765" type="x-p"/> 3. They and their portions shall all be swallowed up. They have <hi type="italic">dealt treacherously against the Lord,</hi> and have thought to strengthen themselves in it by their alliances with strange children; but <hi type="italic">now shall a month devour them with their portions,</hi> that is, their estates and inheritances, all those things which they have taken, and taken up with, as their portion; or by their <hi type="italic">portions</hi> is meant their idols, whom they chose for their portion instead of God. Note, Those that make an idol of the world, by taking it for their portion, will themselves perish with it. A <hi type="italic">month</hi> shall <hi type="italic">devour</hi> them, or eat them up—a certain time prefixed, and a short time. When God's judgments begin with them they shall soon make an end; one month will do their business. How much may a body be weakened by one month's sickness, or a kingdom wasted by one month's war! <hi type="italic">Three shepherds</hi> (says God) <hi type="italic">I cut off in one month,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.11.8">Zech. xi. 8</reference>. Note, The judgments of God sometimes make quick work with a sinful people. A month devours more, and more portions, than many years can repair.
entries.faca6e57953c04f6e90c679c55dd2ff9b7e1a5a0: <div eID="gen19765" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Threatenings of Judgment. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 758.)</title> <div sID="gen19766" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Blow ye the cornet in Gibeah, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the trumpet in Ramah: cry aloud <hi type="italic">at</hi> Beth-aven, after thee, O Benjamin. <hi type="super">9</hi> Ephraim shall be desolate in the day of rebuke: among the tribes of Israel have I made known that which shall surely be. <hi type="super">10</hi> The princes of Judah were like them that remove the bound: <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> I will pour out my wrath upon them like water. <hi type="super">11</hi> Ephraim <hi type="italic">is</hi> oppressed <hi type="italic">and</hi> broken in judgment, because he willingly walked after the commandment. <hi type="super">12</hi> Therefore <hi type="italic">will</hi> I <hi type="italic">be</hi> unto Ephraim as a moth, and to the house of Judah as rottenness. <hi type="super">13</hi> When Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah <hi type="italic">saw</hi> his wound, then went Ephraim to the Assyrian, and sent to king Jareb: yet could he not heal you, nor cure you of your wound. <hi type="super">14</hi> For I <hi type="italic">will be</hi> unto Ephraim as a lion, and as a young lion to the house of Judah: I, <hi type="italic">even</hi> I, will tear and go away; I will take away, and none shall rescue <hi type="italic">him.</hi> <hi type="super">15</hi> I will go <hi type="italic">and</hi> return to my place, till they acknowledge their offence, and seek my face: in their affliction they will seek me early. <div eID="gen19766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19767" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A loud alarm sounded, giving notice of judgments coming (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blow you the cornet in Gibeah</hi> and <hi type="italic">in Ramah,</hi> two cities near together in the confines of the two kingdoms of Judah and Israel, Gibeah a frontier-town of the kingdom of Judah, Ramah of Israel; so that the warning is hereby sent into both kingdoms. "<hi type="italic">Cry aloud at Beth-aven,</hi> or Bethel, which place seems to be already seized upon by the enemy, and therefore the trumpet is not sounded there, but you hear the outcries of those that shout for mastery, mixed with theirs that are overcome." Let them <hi type="italic">cry aloud, "After thee, O Benjamin!</hi> comes the enemy. The tribe of Ephraim is already vanquished, and the enemy will be upon thy back, O Benjamin! in a little time; thy turn comes next. The cup of trembling shall go round." The prophet had described God's controversy with them as a trial at law (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.1">ch. iv. 1</reference>); here he describes it as a trial by battle; and here also <hi type="italic">when he judges he will overcome.</hi> Let all therefore prepare to meet their God. He had before spoken of the judgments as certain; here he speaks of them as near; and, when they are apprehended as just at the door, they are very startling and awakening. The blowing of this cornet is explained, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.9">v. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Among the tribes of Israel have I made known that which shall surely be,</hi> that which is <hi type="italic">true</hi> or <hi type="italic">certain,</hi> so the word is. Note, The destruction of impenitent sinners is a thing which shall surely be; it is not mere talk, to frighten them, but it is an irrevocable sentence. And it is a mercy to us that it is <hi type="italic">made known</hi> to us, that we have timely warning given us of it, that we may <hi type="italic">flee from the wrath to come.</hi> It is the privilege of the tribes of Israel that, as they are told their duty, so they are told their danger, by the oracles of God committed to them. <div eID="gen19767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19768" type="x-p"/> II. The ground of God's controversy with them. 1. He has a quarrel with <hi type="italic">the princes of Judah,</hi> because they were daring leaders in sin, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.10">v. 10</reference>. They are <hi type="italic">like those that remove the bound,</hi> or the ancient land-marks. God has given them his law, to be a fence about his own property; but they have sacrilegiously broken through it, and set it aside; they have encroached even upon God's rights, have trampled upon the distinctions between good and evil, and the most sacred obligations of reason and equity, thinking, because they were princes, that they might do any thing, <hi type="italic">Quicquid libet, licet—Their will was a law.</hi> Or it may be understood of their invading the liberty and property of the subject for the advancing of the prerogative, which was like removing the ancient land-marks. Some have observed that the princes of Judah were more absolute, and assumed a more arbitrary power, than the princes of Israel did; now, for this, God has a controversy with them: <hi type="italic">I will pour out my wrath upon them like water,</hi> in great abundance, like the waters of the flood, which were poured upon the <hi type="italic">giants</hi> of the <hi type="italic">old world,</hi> for the violence which the earth was filled with through them, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.13">Gen. vi. 13</reference>. Note, There are <hi type="italic">bounds</hi> which even princes themselves must not remove, bounds both of religion and justice, which they are limited by, and, if they break through them, they must know that there is a God above them that will call them to account for it. 2. He has a quarrel with the <hi type="italic">people of Ephraim,</hi> because they were sneaking followers in sin (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">He willingly walked after the commandment,</hi> that is, the commandment of Jeroboam and the succeeding kings of Israel, who obliged all their subjects by a law to worship the calves at Dan and Bethel, and never to go up to Jerusalem to worship. This was <hi type="italic">the commandment;</hi> it was the law of the land, and backed with reasons of state; and the people not only walked after it in a blind implicit obedience to authority, but they willingly walked after it, from a secret antipathy they had to the worship of idols. Note, An easy compliance with the commandments of men that thwart the commandments of God ripens a people for ruin as much as any thing. And the punishment of the sequacious disobedience (if I may so call it) answers to the sin; for it is for this that <hi type="italic">Ephraim is oppressed and broken in judgment,</hi> has all his civil rights and liberties broken in upon and trodden down; and, (1.) It is just with God that it should be so, that those who betray God's property should lose their own, that those who subject their consciences to an infallible judge, and an arbitrary power, should have enough of both. (2.) There is a natural tendency in the thing itself towards it. <hi type="italic">Those</hi> that <hi type="italic">willingly walk after the commandment,</hi> even when it walks contrary to the command of God, will find the commandment an encroaching thing, and that the more power is given it the more it will claim. Note, Nothing gives greater advantage to a mastiff-like tyranny, that is fierce and furious, than a spaniel-like submission, that is fawning and flattering. Thus is <hi type="italic">Ephraim oppressed and broken in judgment,</hi> that is, he is wronged under a face and colour of right. Note, It is a sad and sore judgment upon any people to be oppressed under pretence of having justice done them. This explains the threatening <reference osisRef="Hos.5.9">v. 9</reference>, <hi type="italic">Ephraim shall be desolate in the day of rebuke.</hi> Note, Daring sinners must expect that a day of rebuke will come, and such a day of rebuke as will make them desolate, will deprive them of the comfort of all they have and all they hope for. <div eID="gen19768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19769" type="x-p"/> III. The different methods that God would take both with Judah and Ephraim, sometimes one method and sometimes the other, and sometimes both together, or rather by which, first the one and then the other, he would advance towards their complete ruin. <div eID="gen19769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19770" type="x-p"/> 1. He would begin with less judgments, which should sometimes work silently and insensibly (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will be</hi> (that is, my providences shall be) <hi type="italic">unto Ephraim as a moth;</hi> nay (as it might better be supplied), they <hi type="italic">are unto Ephraim as a moth,</hi> for it is such <hi type="italic">a sickness</hi> as Ephraim now sees, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.13">v. 13</reference>. Note, The judgments of God are sometimes to a sinful people <hi type="italic">as a moth,</hi> and <hi type="italic">as rottenness,</hi> or as <hi type="italic">a worm.</hi> The former signifies the little animals that breed in clothes, the latter those that breed in wood; as these consume the clothes and the wood, so shall the judgments of God consume them. (1.) Silently, so as not to make any noise in the world, nay, so as they themselves shall not be sensible of it; they shall think themselves safe and thriving, but, when they come to look more narrowly into their state, shall find themselves wasting and decaying. (2.) Slowly, and with long delays and intervals, that he may give them <hi type="italic">space to repent.</hi> Many a nation, as well as many a person, in the prime of its time, dies of a consumption. (3.) Gradually. God comes upon sinners with less judgments, so to prevent greater, if they will be wise and take warning; he comes upon them step by step, to show he is not willing that they should perish. (4.) The moth breeds in the clothes, and the worm or rottenness in the wood; thus sinners are consumed by a fire of their own kindling. <div eID="gen19770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19771" type="x-p"/> 2. When it appeared that those had not done their work he would come upon them with greater (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will be unto Ephraim as a lion, and to the house of Judah as a young lion,</hi> though Judah is himself, in Jacob's blessing, a <hi type="italic">lion's whelp.</hi> Lest any should think his power weakened, because he was said to be <hi type="italic">as a moth</hi> to them, he says that he will now be as <hi type="italic">a lion</hi> to them, not only to frighten them with his roaring, but to pull them to pieces. Note, If less judgments prevail not to do their work, it may be expected that God will send greater. <hi type="italic">Christ</hi> is sometimes a lion of the tribe of Judah, here he is a lion against that tribe. See what God will do to a people that are secure in sin: <hi type="italic">Even I will tear.</hi> He seems to glory in it, as his prerogative, to be able to <hi type="italic">destroy,</hi> as the <hi type="italic">alone lawgiver,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.4.12">Jam. iv. 12</reference>. "<hi type="italic">I, even I,</hi> will take the work into my own hands; I <hi type="italic">say it</hi> that will <hi type="italic">do it.</hi>" There is a more immediate work of God in some judgments than in others. <hi type="italic">I will tear, and go away.</hi> He will go away, (1.) As not fearing them; he will go away in state, and with a majestic face, as the lion from his prey. (2.) As not helping them. If God tear by afflicting providences, and yet by his graces and comforts stays with us, it is well enough; but our condition is sad indeed if he <hi type="italic">tear</hi> and <hi type="italic">go away,</hi> if, when he deprives us of our creature comforts, he does himself depart from us. When he goes away he will take away all that is valuable and dear, for, when God goes, all good goes along with him. He will take away, <hi type="italic">and none shall rescue him,</hi> as the prey cannot be rescued from the lion, <reference osisRef="Mic.5.8">Mic. v. 8</reference>. Note, None can be delivered out of the hands of God's justice but those that are delivered into the hands of his grace. It is in vain for a man to strive with his Maker. <div eID="gen19771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19772" type="x-p"/> IV. The different effects of those different methods. 1. When God contended with them by less judgments they neglected him, and sought to creatures for relief, but sought in vain, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.13">v. 13</reference>. When God was to them <hi type="italic">as a moth,</hi> and <hi type="italic">as rottenness,</hi> they perceived <hi type="italic">their sickness</hi> and <hi type="italic">their wound;</hi> after a while they found themselves going down the hill, and that they were behind—hand in their affairs, their estate was sensibly decaying, and then they sent <hi type="italic">to the Assyrian,</hi> to come in to their assistance, made their court to king Jareb, which some think, was one of the names of Pul, or Tiglathpileser, kings of Assyria, to whom both Israel and Judah applied for relief in their distress, hoping by an alliance with them to repair and re-establish their declining interests. Note, Carnal hearts, in time of trouble, see their sickness and see their wound, but do not see the sin that is the cause of it, nor will be brought to acknowledge that, no, nor to acknowledge the hand of God, his <hi type="italic">mighty hand,</hi> much less his righteous hand, in their trouble; and therefore, instead of going the next way to the Creator, who could relieve them, they take a great deal of pains to go about to creatures, who can do them no service. Those who repent not that they have offended God by their sins are loth to be beholden to him in their afflictions, but would rather seek relief any where than with him. And what is the consequence? <hi type="italic">Yet could he not heal you, nor cure you of your wound.</hi> Note, Those who neglect God, and seek to creatures for help, will certainly be disappointed; those who depend upon them for support will find them, not <hi type="italic">foundations,</hi> but <hi type="italic">broken reeds;</hi> those who depend upon them for supply will find them, not <hi type="italic">fountains,</hi> but <hi type="italic">broken cisterns;</hi> those who depend upon them for comfort and a cure will find them <hi type="italic">miserable comforters,</hi> and <hi type="italic">physicians of no value.</hi> The kings of Assyria, whom Judah and Israel sought unto, <hi type="italic">distressed them</hi> and <hi type="italic">helped them not,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.16">2 Chron. xxviii. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.28">28</reference>. Some make king <hi type="italic">Jareb</hi> to signify the <hi type="italic">great, potent,</hi> or <hi type="italic">magnificent king,</hi> for they built much upon his power; others <hi type="italic">the king that will plead,</hi> or <hi type="italic">should plead,</hi> for they built much upon his wisdom and eloquence, and in his interesting himself in their affairs. They had sent him <hi type="italic">a present</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.6">ch. x. 6</reference>), a good fee, and, having so retained him of counsel for them, they doubted not of his fidelity to them; but he deceived them, as an arm of flesh does those that trust in it, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.5-Jer.17.6">Jer. xvii. 5, 6</reference>. 2. When, to convince them of their folly, God brought greater judgments upon them, then they would at length be forced to apply to him, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.15">v. 15</reference>. When he has <hi type="italic">torn</hi> as a <hi type="italic">lion,</hi> (1.) He will leave them: <hi type="italic">I will go and return to my place,</hi> to heaven, or to the mercy-seat, the throne of grace, which is his glory. When God punishes sinners he <hi type="italic">comes out of his place</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">Isa. xxvi. 21</reference>); but, when he designs them favour, he <hi type="italic">returns to his place,</hi> where he <hi type="italic">waits to be gracious,</hi> upon their submission. Or he will <hi type="italic">return to his place</hi> when he has corrected them, as not regarding them, hiding his face from them, and not taking notice of their troubles or prayers; and this for their further humiliation, till they are qualified in some measure for the returns of his favour. (2.) He will at length work upon them, and bring them home to himself, by their afflictions, which is the thing he waits for; and then he will no longer withdraw from them. Two things are here mentioned as instances of their return:— [1.] Their penitent confession of sin: <hi type="italic">Till they acknowledge their offence;</hi> marg. <hi type="italic">Till they be guilty,</hi> that is, till they be sensible of their guilt, and be brought to own it, and humble themselves before God for it. Note, When men begin to complain more of their sins than of their afflictions then there begins to be some hope of them; and this is that which God requires of us, when we are under his correcting hand, that we own ourselves in a fault and justly corrected. [2.] Their humble petition for the favour of God: Till they <hi type="italic">seek my face,</hi> which, it may be expected, they will do when they are brought to the last extremity, and they have tried other helpers in vain. <hi type="italic">In their affliction they will seek me early,</hi> that is, diligently and earnestly, and with great importunity; and if they seek him thus, and be sincere in it, though it might be called seeking him late, because it was long ere they were brought to it, yet it is not too late, nay, he is pleased to call it seeking him early, so willing is he to make the best of true penitents in their return to him. Note, When we are under the convictions of sin, and the corrections of the rod, our business is to seek God's face; we must desire the knowledge of him, and an acquaintance with him, that he may manifest himself to us, and for us, in token of his being at peace with us. And it may reasonably be expected that affliction will bring those to God that had long gone astray from him, and kept at a distance. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> God for a time turns away from us, that he may turn us to himself, and then return to us. <hi type="italic">Is any among you afflicted? Let him pray.</hi>  <chapter eID="Hos.5"/> <div eID="gen19772" type="x-p"/>

entries.8cd6fe8d9207165225e86f969388f0c7a8c36c60: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12296"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hos.5.1-Hos.5.5">Ho 5:1-5</reference>. God's Judgments on the Priests, People, and Princes of Israel for Their Sins.</title> <div sID="gen22417" type="x-p"/> Judah, too, being guilty shall be punished; nor shall Assyria, whose aid they both sought, save them; judgments shall at last lead them to repentance.<div eID="gen22417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22418" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12296"/><hi type="bold">1. the king--</hi>probably Pekah; the contemporary of Ahaz, king of Judah, under whom idolatry was first carried so far in Judah as to call for the judgment of the joint Syrian and Israelite invasion, as also that of Assyria.<div eID="gen22418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22419" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment is towards you--</hi>that is, threatens you from God.<div eID="gen22419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22420" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye have been a snare on Mizpah ... net ... upon Tabor--</hi>As hunters spread their net and snares on the hills, Mizpah and Tabor, so ye have snared the people into idolatry and made them your prey by injustice. As Mizpah and Tabor mean a "watch tower," and a "lofty place," a fit scene for hunters, playing on the words, the prophet implies, in the lofty place in which I have set you, whereas ye ought to have been the watchers of the people, guarding them from evil, ye have been as hunters entrapping them into it [Jerome]. These two places are specified, Mizpah in the east and Tabor in the west, to include the high places throughout the whole kingdom, in which Israel's rulers set up idolatrous altars. <div eID="gen22420" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f911687694343f00d0f264df016d4b459c57bbc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12297"/><div sID="gen22421" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12297"/><hi type="bold">2. revolters--</hi>apostates.<div eID="gen22421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22422" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">profound--</hi>deeply rooted [Calvin] and sunk to the lowest depths, excessive in their idolatry (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.9">Ho 9:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.31.6">Is 31:6</reference>) [Henderson]. From the antithesis (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.3">Ho 5:3</reference>), "not hid from me," I prefer explaining, profoundly cunning in their idolatry. Jeroboam thought it a profound piece of policy to set up golden calves to represent God in Dan and Beth-el, in order to prevent Israel's heart from turning again to David's line by going up to Jerusalem to worship. So Israel's subsequent idolatry was grounded by their leaders on various pleas of state expediency (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.29.15">Is 29:15</reference>).<div eID="gen22422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22423" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to ... slaughter--</hi>He does not say "to sacrifice," for their so-called sacrifices were butcheries rather than sacrifices; there was nothing sacred about them, being to idols instead of to the holy God.<div eID="gen22423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22424" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">though--</hi>Maurer translates, "and (in spite of their hope of safety through their slaughter of victims to idols) I will be a chastisement to them all." English Version is good sense: They have deeply revolted, notwithstanding all my prophetical warnings. <div eID="gen22424" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f2fd198c7145e8402250b991c208097ca2a105d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12298"/><div sID="gen22425" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12298"/><hi type="bold">3. Ephraim--</hi>the tribe so called, as distinguished from "Israel" here, the other nine tribes. It was always foremost of the tribes of the northern kingdom. For four hundred years in early history, it, with Manasseh and Benjamin, its two dependent tribes, held the pre-eminence in the whole nation. Ephraim is here addressed as foremost in idolatry.<div eID="gen22425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22426" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I how ... not hid from me--</hi>notwithstanding their supposed profound cunning (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.2">Ho 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.2">Re 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.13">9, 13</reference>, 19).<div eID="gen22426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22427" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">now--</hi>"though I have been a rebuker of all them" (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.2">Ho 5:2</reference>) who commit such spiritual whoredoms, thou art now continuing in them. <div eID="gen22427" type="x-p"/>
entries.4e192a03d40dcc9075c7a0745559bbf70b765ad9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12299"/><div sID="gen22428" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12299"/><hi type="bold">4. They--</hi>Turning from a direct address to Ephraim, he uses the third person plural to characterize the people in general. The Hebrew is against the Margin, their doings will not suffer them" the omission of "them" in the Hebrew after the verb being unusual. The sense is, they are incurable, for they will not permit (as the Hebrew literally means) their doings to be framed so as to turn unto God. Implying that they resist the Spirit of God, not suffering Him to renew them; and give themselves up to "the spirit of whoredoms" (in antithesis to "the Spirit of God" implied in "suffer" or "permit") (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.12">Ho 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.10">Is 63:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.43">Eze 16:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.51">Ac 7:51</reference>). <div eID="gen22428" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb1832667e9b97c0eb85cbf8a0cde194f8eee021: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12300"/><div sID="gen22429" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12300"/><hi type="bold">5. the pride of Israel--</hi>wherewith they reject the warnings of God's prophets (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.2">Ho 5:2</reference>), and prefer their idols to God (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.10">Ho 7:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.13.17">Jr 13:17</reference>).<div eID="gen22429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22430" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">testify to his face--</hi>openly to his face he shall be convicted of the pride which is so palpable in him. Or, "in his face," as in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.9">Is 3:9</reference>.<div eID="gen22430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22431" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Judah ... shall fall with them--</hi>This prophecy is later than <reference osisRef="Hos.4.15">Ho 4:15</reference>, when Judah had not gone so far in idolatry; now her imitation of Israel's bad example provokes the threat of her being doomed to share in Israel's punishment. <div eID="gen22431" type="x-p"/>
entries.bdcbb46d90e96478cdd82986dbb84a52c23e15b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12301"/><div sID="gen22432" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12301"/><hi type="bold">6. with ... flocks--</hi>to propitiate Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.11-Isa.1.15">Is 1:11-15</reference>).<div eID="gen22432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22433" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seek ... not find--</hi>because it is slavish fear that leads them to seek Him; and because it then shall be too late (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.28">Pr 1:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.34">Joh 7:34</reference>). <div eID="gen22433" type="x-p"/>
entries.12512585600ca99fa44c9c00e4791c82d62798ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12302"/><div sID="gen22434" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12302"/><hi type="bold">7. treacherously--</hi>as to the marriage covenant (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.20">Jr 3:20</reference>).<div eID="gen22434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22435" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strange children--</hi>alluding to "children of whoredoms" (<reference osisRef="Hos.1.2">Ho 1:2</reference>; 2:4). "Strange" or foreign implies that their idolatry was imported from abroad [Henderson]. Or rather, "regarded by God as strangers, not His," as being reared in idolatry. The case is desperate, when not only the existing, but also the rising, generation is reared in apostasy.<div eID="gen22435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22436" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a month--</hi>a very brief space of time shall elapse, and then punishment shall overtake them (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.8">Zec 11:8</reference>). The allusion seems to be to money loans, which were by the month, not as with us by the year. You cannot put it off; the time of your destruction is immediately and suddenly coming on you; just as the debtor must meet the creditor's demand at the expiration of the month. The prediction is of the invasion of Tiglath-pileser, who carried away Reuben, Gad, Naphtali, and the half tribe of Manasseh.<div eID="gen22436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22437" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">portions--</hi>that is, possessions. Their resources and garrisons will not avail to save them. Henderson explains from <reference osisRef="Isa.57.6">Is 57:6</reference>, "portions" as their idols; the context favors this, "the Lord" the true "portion of His people" (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.9">De 32:9</reference>), being in antithesis to "their portions," the idols. <div eID="gen22437" type="x-p"/>
entries.a6e9924ae5e85d10e3cdbed17074e8a0960d973e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12303"/><div sID="gen22438" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12303"/>8. The arrival of the enemy is announced in the form of an injunction to blow an alarm.<div eID="gen22438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22439" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cornet ... trumpet--</hi>The "cornet" was made of the curved horn of animals and was used by shepherds. The "trumpet" was of brass or silver, straight, and used in wars and on solemn occasions. The Hebrew is hatzotzerah, the sound imitating the trumpet note (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.1">Ho 8:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.10.2">Nu 10:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.5">Jr 4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.1">Joe 2:1</reference>).<div eID="gen22439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22440" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gibeah ... Ramah--</hi>both in Benjamin (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.29">Is 10:29</reference>).<div eID="gen22440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22441" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Beth-aven--</hi>in Benjamin; not as in <reference osisRef="Hos.4.15">Ho 4:15</reference>; Beth-el, but a town east of it (<reference osisRef="Josh.7.2">Jos 7:2</reference>). "Cry aloud," namely, to raise the alarm. "Benjamin" is put for the whole southern kingdom of Judah (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.5.5">Ho 5:5</reference>), being the first part of it which would meet the foe advancing from the north. "After thee, O Benjamin," implies the position of Beth-aven, behind Benjamin, at the borders of Ephraim. When the foe is at Beth-aven, he is at Benjamin's rear, close upon thee, O Benjamin (<reference osisRef="Judg.5.14">Jud 5:14</reference>). <div eID="gen22441" type="x-p"/>
entries.6dfc4e362eb8d07ab31b32e5f211d1de8a418ff2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12304"/><div sID="gen22442" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12304"/>9-10. Israel is referred to in <reference osisRef="Hos.5.9">Ho 5:9</reference>, Judah in <reference osisRef="Hos.5.10">Ho 5:10</reference>.<div eID="gen22442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22443" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the day of rebuke--</hi>the day when I shall chastise him.<div eID="gen22443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22444" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among the tribes of Israel have I made known--</hi>proving that the scene of Hosea's labor was among the ten tribes.<div eID="gen22444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22445" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that which shall surely be--</hi>namely, the coming judgment here foretold. It is no longer a conditional decree, leaving a hope of pardon on repentance; it is absolute, for Ephraim is hopelessly impenitent. <div eID="gen22445" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d19ae612a6153c0ecf6163ea2ece9cad0ba9fe0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12306"/><div sID="gen22447" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12306"/><hi type="bold">11. broken in judgment--</hi>namely, the "judgment" of God on him (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.1">Ho 5:1</reference>).<div eID="gen22447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walked after the commandment--</hi>Jeroboam's, to worship the calves (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.28-2Kgs.10.33">2Ki 10:28-33</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Mic.6.16">Mi 6:16</reference>, "the statutes of Omri," namely, idolatrous statutes. We ought to obey God rather than men (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.29">Ac 5:29</reference>). Jerome reads "filthiness." The Septuagint gives the sense, not the literal translation: "after vanities." <div eID="gen22448" type="x-p"/>
entries.34e0c8678f0059e3d7d6d6d4954b522cee3974b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12307"/><div sID="gen22449" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12307"/><hi type="bold">12. as a moth--</hi>consuming a garment (<reference osisRef="Job.13.28">Job 13:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.39.11">Psa 39:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.50.9">Is 50:9</reference>).<div eID="gen22449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22450" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Judah ... rottenness--</hi>Ephraim, or the ten tribes, are as a garment eaten by the moth; Judah as the body itself consumed by rottenness (<reference osisRef="Prov.12.4">Pr 12:4</reference>). Perhaps alluding to the superiority of the latter in having the house of David, and the temple, the religious center of the nation [Grotius]. As in <reference osisRef="Hos.5.13">Ho 5:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.14">14</reference>, the violence of the calamity is prefigured by the "wound" which "a lion" inflicts, so here its long protracted duration, and the certainty and completeness of the destruction from small unforeseen beginnings, by the images of a slowly but surely consuming moth and rottenness. <div eID="gen22450" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf4ff842b626b9e12a47f27536b294b98eda9bb2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12308"/><div sID="gen22451" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12308"/><hi type="bold">13. wound--</hi>literally, "bandage"; hence a bandaged wound (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">Is 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.12">Jr 30:12</reference>). "Saw," that is, felt its weakened state politically, and the dangers that threatened it. It aggravates their perversity, that, though aware of their unsound and calamitous state, they did not inquire into the cause or seek a right remedy.<div eID="gen22451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22452" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went ... to the Assyrian--</hi>First, Menahem (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.19">2Ki 15:19</reference>) applied to Pul; again, Hoshea to Shalmaneser (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.3">2Ki 17:3</reference>).<div eID="gen22452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22453" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sent to King Jareb--</hi>Understand Judah as the nominative to "sent." Thus, as "Ephraim saw his sickness" (the first clause) answers in the parallelism to "Ephraim went to the Assyrian" (the third clause), so "Judah saw his wound" (the second clause) answers to (Judah) "sent to King Jareb" (the fourth clause). Jareb ought rather to be translated, "their defender," literally, "avenger" [Jerome]. The Assyrian "king," ever ready, for his own aggrandizement, to mix himself up with the affairs of neighboring states, professed to undertake Israel's and Judah's cause; in <reference osisRef="Judg.6.32">Jud 6:32</reference>, Jerub, in Jerub-baal is so used, namely, "plead one's cause." Judah, under Ahaz, applied to Tiglath-pileser for aid against Syria and Israel (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.7">2Ki 16:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.16-2Chr.28.21">2Ch 28:16-21</reference>); the Assyrian "distressed him, but strengthened him not," fulfiling the prophecy here, "he could not heal you, nor cure you of your wound. <div eID="gen22453" type="x-p"/>
entries.b90382a496c4ae81239cc4b74ddcf88be28bbc28: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12309"/><div sID="gen22454" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12309"/><hi type="bold">14. lion--</hi>The black lion and the young lion are emblems of strength and ferocity (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.13">Psa 91:13</reference>).<div eID="gen22454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22455" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I, even I--</hi>emphatic; when I, even I, the irresistible God, tear in pieces (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.22">Psa 50:22</reference>), no Assyrian power can rescue.<div eID="gen22455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22456" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go away--</hi>as a lion stalks leisurely back with his prey to his lair. <div eID="gen22456" type="x-p"/>
entries.6015fc4bb19166d7d9febbf1b93770dbe154d70f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12310"/><div sID="gen22457" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12310"/><hi type="bold">15. return to my place--</hi>that is, withdraw My favor.<div eID="gen22457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22458" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">till they acknowledge their offence--</hi>The Hebrew is, "till they suffer the penalty of their guilt." Probably "accepting the punishment of their guilt" (compare <reference osisRef="Zech.11.5">Zec 11:5</reference>) is included in the idea, as English Version translates. Compare <reference osisRef="Lev.26.40">Le 26:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.41">41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.12">Jr 29:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.9">Eze 6:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.43">20:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.31">36:31</reference>.<div eID="gen22458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22459" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seek my face--</hi>that is, seek My favor (<reference osisRef="Prov.29.26">Pr 29:26</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen22459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22460" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... affliction ... seek me early--</hi>that is, diligently; rising up before dawn to seek Me (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.147">Psa 119:147</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.78.34">Psa 78:34</reference>). <chapter eID="Hos.5"/>

entries.a4dffc5c5136a910ca693f70031f0a5b19c1fde4: <div eID="gen33660" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33661" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33662" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33662" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33661" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33663" type="x-p"/> This chapter begins with threatening the Israelites for ensnaring the people to idolatry by their sacrifices and other rites on Mizpah and Tabor, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.1-Hos.5.5">Hos 5:1-5</reference>. Their sacrifices, however costly, are declared to be unacceptable, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.6">Hos 5:6</reference>; and their substance is devoted to the locust, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.7">Hos 5:7</reference>. Nor is judgment to stop here. The cities of Judah are called upon, in a very animated manner, to prepare for the approach of enemies. Benjamin is to be pursued; Ephraim is to be desolate; and all this is intimated to Israel, that they may by repentance avert the judgment, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.8">Hos 5:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.9">Hos 5:9</reference>. The following verses contain farther denunciations, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.10-Hos.5.13">Hos 5:10-13</reference>, expressed in terms equally terrible and sublime, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.14">Hos 5:14</reference>. The Lord afflicts not willingly the children of men; he visits them with temporal calamities that he may heal their spiritual malady, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.15">Hos 5:15</reference>. <div eID="gen33663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33664" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen33664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33665" type="x-p"/> Hear ye this, O priests - A process is instituted against the priests, the Israelites, and the house of the king; and they are called on to appear and defend themselves. The accusation is, that they have ensnared the people, caused them to practice idolatry, both at Mizpah and Tabor. Mizpah was situated beyond Jordan; in the mountains of Gilead; see <reference osisRef="Jdg.11.29">Jdg 11:29</reference>. And Tabor was a beautiful mountain in the tribe of Zebulum. Both these places are said to be eminent for hunting etc., and hence the natural occurrence of the words snare and net, in speaking of them.
entries.b905f74e35cfa4c4043e927203e32921e73b37b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen33665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33666" type="x-p"/> The revolters are profound to make slaughter - Here may be a reference to the practice of hunters, making deep pits in the ground, and lightly covering them over, that the beasts, not discovering them, might fall in, and become a prey. <div eID="gen33666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33667" type="x-p"/> Though I have been a Rebuker - "I will bring chastisement on them all." As they have made victims of others to their idolatry, I will make victims of them to my justice. Some have thought that as many as wished to depart from the idolatrous worship set up by Jeroboam, were slaughtered; and thus Jeroboam the son of Nebat Made Israel to sin.
entries.b932d3c950e1160af00354bb22b4d3c5255eff4d: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen33667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33668" type="x-p"/> I know Ephraim - I know the whole to be idolaters.
entries.8de4692860da44f078e58e0b93ee8688c68e60cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen33668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33669" type="x-p"/> They will not frame their doings - They never purpose to turn to God, they have fully imbibed the spirit of idolatry.
entries.013ef5fd0a224890a3dc082915188e950b9d5794: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen33669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33670" type="x-p"/> The pride of Israel doth testify to his face - The effrontery with which they practise idolatry manifests, not only their insolence, but the deep depravity of their heart; but their pride and arrogance shall be humbled.
entries.4d176635bdb5a8e627ada501c89ab02843e82cea: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen33670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33671" type="x-p"/> They shall go with their flocks - They shall offer many sacrifices, professing to seek and be reconciled to the Lord; but they shall not find him. As they still retain the spirit of their idolatry, he has withdrawn himself from them.
entries.e22014dd0530717bbc729a5329b74592b508f004: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen33671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33672" type="x-p"/> Now shall a month devour them - In a month's time the king of Assyria shall be upon them, and oblige them to purchase their lives and liberties by a grievous tax of fifty shekels per head. This Menahem, king of Israel, gave to Pul, king of Assyria, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.16-2Kgs.15.20">2Kgs 15:16-20</reference>. Instead of month, some translate the original locust. "The locusts shall devour them."
entries.03130dbdaa83facec59c13f4b6478feecf7ee593: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen33672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33673" type="x-p"/> Blow ye the cornet in Gibeah - Gibeah and Ramah were cities of Judah, in the tribe of Benjamin. <div eID="gen33673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33674" type="x-p"/> After thee, O Benjamin - An abrupt call of warning. "Benjamin, fly for thy life! The enemy is just behind thee!" This is a prediction of the invasion of the Assyrians, and the captivity of the ten tribes.
entries.549b68d088f13fa7387d01a989b450f9f4a3bf74: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen33674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33675" type="x-p"/> Among the tribes of Israel have I made known - They have got sufficient warning; it is their own fault that they have not taken it.
entries.c18987b78ee3dd7e17e2cc55ecd5929b0104c49d: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen33675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33676" type="x-p"/> Like them that remove the bound - As execrable as they who remove the land-mark. They have leaped over law's enclosure, and scaled all the walls of right; they have despised and broken all laws, human and Divine.
entries.6ca0b67da72f36a2c079ae7405cdc2e959310136: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen33676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33677" type="x-p"/> Walked after the commandment - Jeroboam's commandment to worship his calves at Dan and Beth-el. Many of them were not forced to do this, they did it willingly.
entries.eddae869bbcb070ca5863209813c811c8ac6b1ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen33677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33678" type="x-p"/> Unto Ephraim as a moth - I will consume them by little and little, as a moth frets a garment.
entries.cd7c09447c71dc85ed09a62acf29507d44680ae8: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen33678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33679" type="x-p"/> When Ephraim saw his sickness - When both Israel and Judah felt their own weakness to resist their enemies, instead of calling upon and trusting in me, they sought sinful alliances, and trusted in their idols. <div eID="gen33679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33680" type="x-p"/> King Jareb - This name occurs nowhere in Scripture but here and in <reference osisRef="Hos.10.6">Hos 10:6</reference>. The Vulgate and Targum render ירב yareb, an avenger, a person whom they thought able to save them from their enemies. It is well known that Menahem, king of Israel, sought alliance with Pul and Tiglath-pileser, kings of Assyria, and Ahaz, king of Judah. These were the protectors that Ephraim sought after. See 2 Kings 15 and 16. But far from healing them by making them tributary, the Assyrians made their wound more dangerous.
entries.0f213a4b688e4b75beaa1fd50c12ce4dfa8fca15: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen33680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33681" type="x-p"/> I will be - as a lion - כשחל cashshachel, as a panther or lioness.
entries.090577e0971c32ced8467adb0683f9c12cb04c51: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen33681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33682" type="x-p"/> I will go and return to my place - I will abandon them till they acknowledge their offenses. This had the wished-for effect, as we shall see in the following chapter; for they repented and turned to God, and he had mercy upon them. These two verses are considered as instances of the true sublime.  <chapter eID="Hos.5"/> <div eID="gen33682" type="x-p"/>

entries.82e261ff663a720980282764bd1ed04f49aa4066: Hos 5:1 <div eID="gen16206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16207" type="x-p"/> With the words “Hear ye this,” the reproof of the sins of Israel makes a new start, and is specially addressed to the priests and the king’s house, i.e., the king and his court, to announce to the leaders of the nation the punishment that will follow their apostasy from God and their idolatry, by which they have plunged the people and the kingdom headlong into destruction. Hos 5:1-5 form the first strophe. Hos 5:1. <hi type="italic">“Hear ye this, ye priests; and give heed thereto, O house of Israel; and observe it, O house of the king! for the judgment applies to you; for ye have become a snare at Mizpah, and a net spread upon Tabor.” </hi> By the word “<hi type="italic">this,” </hi>which points back to Hos 5:4, the prophecy that follows is attached to the preceding one. Beside the priests and the king’s house, i.e., the royal family, in which the counsellors and adjutants surrounding the king are probably included, the house of Israel, that is to say, the people of the ten tribes regarded as a family, is summoned to hear, because what was about to be announced applied to the people and kingdom as a whole. There is nothing to warrant our understanding by the “house of Israel,” the heads of the nation or elders. <hi type="italic">Lâkjem hammishpât</hi> does not mean, It rests with you to know or to defend the right; nor, “Ye ought to hear the reproof,” as Hitzig explains it, for <hi type="italic">mishpât</hi> in this connection signifies neither “the maintenance of justice” nor “a reproof,” but the judgment about to be executed by God, τὸ κρίμα (lxx). The thought is this, The judgment will fall upon you; and <hi type="italic">lâkhem</hi> refers chiefly to the priests and the king’s house, as the explanatory clause which follows clearly shows. It is impossible to determine with certainty what king’s house is intended. Probably that of Zechariah or Menahem; possibly both, since Hosea prophesied in both reigns, and merely gives the quintessence of his prophetical addresses in his book. Going to Asshur refers rather to Menahem than to Zechariah (comp. 2Ki 15:19-20). In the figures employed, the bird-trap (<hi type="italic">pach</hi>) and the net spread for catching birds, it can only be the rulers of the nation who are represented as a trap and net, and the birds must denote the people generally who are enticed into the net of destruction and caught (cf. Hos 9:8).<note placement="foot">Jerome has given a very good explanation of the figure: “I have appointed you as watchmen among the people, and set you in the highest place of honour, that ye might govern the erring people; but ye have become a trap, and are to be called sportsmen rather than watchmen.”</note><hi type="italic">Mizpah</hi>, as a parallel to Tabor, can only be the lofty <hi type="italic">Mizpah</hi> of Gilead (Jdg 10:17; Jdg 11:29) or Ramah-Mizpah, which probably stood upon the site of the modern es-Salt (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.4.43">Deu 4:43</reference>); so that, whilst Tabor represents the land on this side of the Jordan, Mizpah, which resembled it in situation, is chosen to represent the land to the east of the river.<note placement="foot">As Tabor, for instance, rises up as a solitary conical hill (see at Jdg 4:6), so es-Salt is built about the sides of a round steep hill, which rises up in a narrow rocky valley, and upon the summit of which there stands a strong fortification (see Seetzen in Burckhardt’s Reisen in Syrien, p. 1061).</note> <div eID="gen16207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16208" type="x-p"/> Both places were probably noted as peculiarly adapted for bird-catching, since Tabor is still thickly wooded. The supposition that they had been used as places of sacrifice in connection with idolatrous worship, cannot be inferred from the verse before us, nor is it rendered probable by other passages.
entries.129bba56a818d44342be9e7d804e9b3eb80fbd34: Hos 5:2 <div eID="gen16208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16209" type="x-p"/> This accusation is still further vindicated in Hos 5:2., by a fuller exposure of the moral corruption of the nation. Hos 5:2. <hi type="italic">“And excesses they have spread out deeply; but I am a chastisement to them all.” </hi> The meaning of the first half of the verse, which is very difficult, and has been very differently interpreted by both ancient and modern expositors, has been brought out best by Delitzsch (Com. on <reference osisRef="Ps.101.3">Psa 101:3</reference>), who renders it, “they understand from the very foundation how to spread out transgressions.” For the word שׂטים the meaning transgressions is well established by the use of סטים in <reference osisRef="Ps.101.3">Psa 101:3</reference>, where Hengstenberg, Hupfeld, and Delitzsch all agree that this is the proper rendering (see Ewald’s philological defence of it at §146, e). In the psalm referred to, however, the expression עשׂה סטים also shows that <hi type="italic">shachătâh</hi> is the inf. <hi type="italic">piel</hi>, and <hi type="italic">sētı̄m</hi> the accusative of the object. And it follows from this that <hi type="italic">shachătâh</hi> neither means to slaughter or slaughter sacrifices, nor can be used for שׁחתה in the sense of acting injuriously, but that it is to be interpreted according to the <hi type="italic">shâchūth</hi> in 1Ki 10:16-17, in the sense of stretching, stretching out; so that there is no necessity to take שׁחט in the sense of שׁטח, as Delitzsch does, though the use of עלוה for עולה in Hos 10:9 may no doubt be adduced in its support. שׂטים, from שׂטה (to turn aside, Num 5:12, Num 5:19), are literally digressions or excesses, answering to the <hi type="italic">hiznâh</hi> in Hos 5:3, the leading sin of Israel. “They have deepened to stretch out excesses,” i.e., they have gone to great lengths, or are deeply sunken in excesses, - a thought quite in harmony with the context, to which the threat is appended. “I (Jehovah) am a chastisement to them all, to the rulers as well as to the people;” i.e., I will punish them all (cf. Hos 5:12), because their idolatrous conduct is well known to me. The way is thus prepared for the two following verses.
entries.b59048e808da6215f2585e794d5da917df5abff6: Hos 5:3-4 <hi type="italic">“I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hid from me: for now, O Ephraim, thou hast committed whoredom; Israel has defiled itself. Hos 5:4. Their works do not allow to return to their God, for the spirit of whoredom is in them, and they know not Jehovah.” </hi> By עתּה, the whoredom of Ephraim is designated as in fact lying before them, and therefore undeniable; but not, as Hitzig supposes, an act which has taken place once for all, viz., the choice of a king, by which the severance of the kingdoms and the previous idolatry had been sanctioned afresh. נטמא, defiled by whoredom, i.e., idolatry. Their works do not allow them to return to their God, because the works are merely an emanation of the character and state of the heart, and in their hearts the demon of whoredom has its seat (cf. Hos 4:12), and the knowledge of the Lord is wanting; that is to say, the demoniacal power of idolatry has taken complete possession of the heart, and stifled the knowledge of the true God. The rendering, “they do not direct their actions to this,” is incorrect, and cannot be sustained by an appeal to the use of נתן לב in Jdg 15:1 and 1Sa 24:8., or to Jdg 3:28.
entries.708afcd29d7717ac0ce35e5735c69f51fd18a2f7: Hos 5:5 <hi type="italic">“And the pride of Ephraim will testify against its face, and Israel and Ephraim will stumble in their guilt; Judah has also stumbled with them.” </hi> As the meaning “to answer,” to bear witness against a person, is well established in the case of ענה ב (cf. Num 35:30; <reference osisRef="Deut.19.18">Deu 19:18</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.3.9">Isa 3:9</reference>), and ענה בפנים also occurs in <reference osisRef="Job.16.8">Job 16:8</reference> in this sense, we must retain the same meaning here, as Jerome and others have done. And there is the more reason for this, because the explanation based upon the lxx, καὶ ταπεινωθήσεται ἡ ὕβρις, “the haughtiness of Israel will be humbled,” can hardly be reconciled with בפניו. “The pride of Israel,” moreover, is not the haughtiness of Israel, but that of which Israel is proud, or rather the glory of Israel. We might understand by this the flourishing condition of the kingdom, after <reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">Amo 6:8</reference>; but it would be only by its decay that this would bear witness against the sin of Israel, so that “the glory of Israel” would stand for “the decay of that glory,” which would be extremely improbable. We must therefore explain “the glory of Israel” here and in Hos 7:10 in accordance with <reference osisRef="Amos.8.7">Amo 8:7</reference>, i.e., we must understand it as referring to Jehovah, who is Israel’s eminence and glory; in which case we obtain the following very appropriate thought: They know not Jehovah, they do not concern themselves about Him; therefore He Himself will bear witness by judgments, by the destruction of their false glory (cf. Hos 2:10-14), against the face of Israel, i.e., bear witness to their face. This thought occurs without ambiguity in Hos 7:10. Israel will stumble in its sin, i.e., will fall and perish (as in Hos 4:5). Judah also falls with Israel, because it has participated in Israel’s sin (Hos 4:15).
entries.bfb7e4e531c7620cbaf60b365896cea3b1d32213: Hos 5:6-7 <div eID="gen16209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16210" type="x-p"/> Israel, moreover, will not be able to avert the threatening judgment by sacrifices. Jehovah will withdraw from the faithless generation, and visit it with His judgments. This is the train of thought in the next strophe (Hos 5:6-10). Hos 5:6. <hi type="italic">“They will go with their sheep and their oxen to seek Jehovah, and will not find Him: He has withdrawn Himself from them. </hi> Hos 5:7. <hi type="italic">They acted treacherously against Jehovah, for they have born strange children: now will the new moon devour them with their fields.” </hi> The offering of sacrifices will be no help to them, because God has withdrawn Himself from them, and does not hear their prayers; for God has no pleasure in sacrifices which are offered in an impenitent state of mind (cf. Hos 6:6; Isa 1:11.; Jer 7:21.; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.7">Psa 50:7</reference>, Psa 50:8.). The reason for this is given in Hos 5:7. <hi type="italic">Bâgad</hi>, to act faithlessly, which is frequently applied to the infidelity of a wife towards her husband (e.g., <reference osisRef="Jer.3.20">Jer 3:20</reference>; Mal 2:14; cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.21.8">Exo 21:8</reference>), points to the conjugal relation in which Israel stood to Jehovah. Hence the figure which follows. “Strange children” are such as do not belong to the home (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.5">Deu 25:5</reference>), i.e., such as have not sprung from the conjugal union. In actual fact, the expression is equivalent to בּני זנוּנים in Hos 1:2; Hos 2:4, though <hi type="italic">zâr</hi> does not expressly mean “adulterous.” Israel ought to have begotten children of God in the maintenance of the covenant with the Lord; but in its apostasy from God it had begotten an adulterous generation, children whom the Lord could not acknowledge as His own. “The new moon will devour them,” viz., those who act so faithlessly. the meaning is not, “they will be destroyed on the next new moon;” but the new moon, as the festal season, on which sacrifices were offered (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.6">1Sa 20:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.29">1Sa 20:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.13-Isa.1.14">Isa 1:13-14</reference>), stands here for the sacrifices themselves that were offered upon it. The meaning is this: your sacrificial feast, your hypocritical worship, so far from bringing you salvation, will rather prove your sin. חלקיהם are not sacrificial portions, but the hereditary portions of Israel, the portions of land that fell to the different families and households, and from the produce of which they offered sacrifices to the Lord.<note placement="foot">It is very evident from this verse, that the feasts and the worship prescribed in the Mosaic law were observed in the kingdom of the ten tribes, at the places of worship in Bethel and Dan.</note>
entries.c499e51b5cfe6c835509a99e7fb6ebbec9c4172e: Hos 5:8 <div eID="gen16210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16211" type="x-p"/> The prophet sees in spirit the judgment already falling upon the rebellious nation, and therefore addresses the following appeal to the people. Hos 5:8. <hi type="italic">“Blow ye the horn at Gibeah, the trumpet at Ramah! Raise the cry at Bethaven, Behind thee, Benjamin!” </hi> The blowing of the <hi type="italic">shōphâr</hi>, a far-sounding horn, or of the trumpet<note placement="foot">“The <hi type="italic">sophar</hi> was a shepherd’s horn, and was made of a carved horn; the <hi type="italic">tuba</hi> (<hi type="italic">chătsōtserâh</hi>) was made of brass or silver, and sounded either in the time of war or at festivals.” - Jerome.</note> (<hi type="italic">chătsōtserâh</hi>), was a signal by which the invasion of foes (Hos 8:1; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.5">Jer 4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.1">Jer 6:1</reference>) and other calamities (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.1">Joe 2:1</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.3.6">Amo 3:6</reference>) were announced, to give the inhabitants warning of the danger that threatened them. The words therefore imply that foes had invaded the land. <hi type="italic">Gibeah</hi> (of Saul; see at <reference osisRef="Josh.18.28">Jos 18:28</reference>) and <hi type="italic">Ramah</hi> (of Samuel; see at <reference osisRef="Josh.18.25">Jos 18:25</reference>) were two elevated places on the northern boundary of the tribe of Benjamin, which were well adapted for signals, on account of their lofty situation. The introduction of these particular towns, which did not belong to the tribe of Israel, but to that of Judah, is intended to intimate that the enemy has already conquered the kingdom of the ten tribes, and has advanced to the border of that of Judah. הריע, to make a noise, is to be understood here as relating to the alarm given by the war-signals already mentioned, as in <reference osisRef="Joel.2.1">Joe 2:1</reference>, cf. Num 10:9. <hi type="italic">Bethaven</hi> is Bethel (Beitin), as in Hos 4:15, the seat of the idolatrous worship of the calves; and בּית is to be taken in the sense of בּבית (according to Ges. §118, 1). The difficult words, “behind thee, Benjamin,” cannot indicate the situation or attitude of Benjamin, in relation to Bethel or the kingdom of Israel, or show that “the invasion is to be expected to start from Benjamin,” as Simson supposes. For the latter is no more appropriate in this train of thought than a merely geographical or historical notice.
